newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Northwest hydropower generation still rising.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Northwest hydropower generation still rising.

text.p: Output of hydroelectric power in the U.S. Pacific Northwest continues to rise as recent heavy precipitation moves downstream, regional industry sources said Thursday.

A "pineapple express" - warm, moist air from Hawaii - collided with a cold front from Canada late Monday, dumping heavy snow on Washington and parts of Idaho, while much of Oregon saw heavy rain and flooding.
The National Weather Service on Thursday forecast continued rain in western Oregon, with the likelihood of more precipitation falling to 50 percent through the weekend.

"Generation is creeping up on us. The in-flows on the Snake (River) were more than we expected," said a trade source at Bonneville Power Administration (BPA), the federal agency which markets electricity produced from U.S. dams in the Northwest.
He explained that northern Idaho and parts of Washington received a lot of snow, which is melting as temperatures rise.
The extra flows on the Snake have crested, and are expected to run through the system within a couple of days, according to the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, which operates the dams.

For Friday schedulings, BPA offered up to 800 MW of firm and non-firm power during light load hours and another 800 MW of firm power during heavy load hours. On Monday, the agency offered only up to 200 MW of firm surplus power.

The BPA source noted that the Snake River connects with the Columbia River south of Vernita Bar, the flat area where daytime flows have been restricted since early October to ensure enough water there for endangered fish to spawn.
The Vernita Bar restrictions are scheduled to end early next week.
The BPA source said a sustained rise in hydroelectric output is unlikely and, although more rain is forecast, it is expected to be less intense and mainly south of the Columbia River basin.
